official_skills.notes: Uses the agentskillsforall CLI, not the skills CLI.
Not published by the Spring team. The install command was not confirmed on 2026-08-27. Present it as a community option with that caveat stated out loud, never as the default.

gap_map.why_it_matters: No skill collection published by the Spring team was found on 2026-08-27. This is the largest gap in the registry: Spring Boot is a heavily convention-driven framework, exactly the kind where a framework-team skill pays the most.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor works from the codebase and consults Spring documentation on demand, and states plainly that no framework-team skill is available. If you find one, open an issue - see CONTRIBUTING.md.

gap_map.why_it_matters: @SpringBootTest is the path of least resistance and boots the whole context for every test. Suites built that way get slow enough that people stop running them, which is worse than having fewer tests.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor applies references/quality-gate.md, and pushes tests down to plain unit tests and slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) unless full-context wiring is the thing under test.

layers.name: unit
layers.belongs_here: business rules with collaborators passed directly - no Spring context at all
layers.does_not_belong_here: anything needing beans wired to prove it
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the test is annotated @SpringBootTest to call one pure method

layers.name: slice
layers.belongs_here: one layer with only the beans it needs: @WebMvcTest for controllers, @DataJpaTest for repositories, @JsonTest for serialization
layers.cost: moderate; the context is small and cached
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the slice annotation was replaced with @SpringBootTest because something was missing - that is a design signal, not a test problem

layers.name: integration
layers.belongs_here: the full context via @SpringBootTest, for wiring and cross-layer behaviour
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: every test in the suite is @SpringBootTest and the suite now takes minutes

testing.proportions: Spring Boot team: auto-configuration 'can sometimes be a little too much for tests', and it 'often helps to load only the parts of the configuration that are required to test a slice of your application'. Slices are also faster because Spring caches contexts and a smaller context is cached and reused.
rules: Reach for a slice before @SpringBootTest. The framework's own guidance is to load only the parts a test needs.
Tests that share the same configuration reuse a cached context. Every distinct configuration is another context boot, so gratuitous @MockBean variation silently multiplies the suite's runtime.
A rule that needs no Spring beans gets a plain JUnit test with no annotations at all.
Use the Maven or Gradle wrapper that exists in the repository. Never both.
Slice tests do not load your security configuration by default - an endpoint that looks authorized in @WebMvcTest may be open in production.
traps: @SpringBootTest everywhere: the suite gets slow enough that people stop running it, which is worse than having fewer tests.
Context caching hides the cost until a small annotation change forces a new context and the suite time doubles with no obvious cause.
@MockBean changes the context signature, so each unique combination is a separate cached context.
@Transactional on a test rolls back what the production code would have committed, so a test passes on code that would fail for real.
Component scan means a bean added anywhere joins every context - a test can pass because of a bean nobody intended to include.
Lazy loading works under an open session in a test and throws in production where the session is already closed.
what_not_to_test: That Spring injects a bean, or that @RestController maps a route.
Flyway or Liquibase migration files as units - run them instead.
Configuration property binding, unless the binding itself has custom logic.
testing.notes: Pick the Maven or Gradle command by which wrapper exists in the repository; never run both. Slice tests (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest) are the layer this stack most often skips and most needs.

growth_thresholds.extract_service_layer: a controller method exceeds 30 lines, which means business logic has leaked into the transport layer

layers.name: Controller
layers.holds: transport: request mapping, validation, response shaping
layers.must_not: hold business rules - a controller method past 30 lines has absorbed the service

layers.name: Service
layers.holds: business rules and the transaction boundary
layers.must_not: know about HttpServletRequest or status codes

layers.name: Domain / entity
layers.must_not: be the API contract - expose DTOs, not entities

variants.name: Package by feature
variants.use_when: the default; each feature owns its controller, service and repository
variants.cost: a rule shared by two features needs a deliberate home

variants.name: Package by layer
variants.use_when: very small applications, or a team that already works this way
variants.cost: every feature change touches every package, and the boundaries mean nothing

rules: Package by feature, not by layer. A change to one feature should touch one package.
Entities are never returned from a controller. A JPA entity as an API response leaks the schema and lazy-loads at serialization time.
The transaction boundary is on the service, not the repository and not the controller.
A service never imports the servlet API.
Component scan makes wiring invisible: a bean that is never imported by name is still live. Anything conditional (@Profile, @ConditionalOnProperty) belongs in CLAUDE.md.
architecture.notes: Spring Boot documents structuring your code in a main-application-class package, but does not mandate package-by-feature. That preference is the mentor's judgment - present it as such. This is the only stack in the registry with no framework-team skill collection.

key_decisions.decision: Package by feature or by layer
key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Spring Boot mandates neither, and the choice is close to irreversible once a codebase has grown.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: By feature. A change to one feature should touch one package.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: By-layer packaging means every feature change touches every package, and no boundary can be enforced later without moving every file.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: @Transactional works on any layer and nothing tells you which one is right.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A boundary on the repository means each write commits separately, so a half-completed operation is already durable.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Returning entities directly works and is the fastest thing to write.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Entities as responses leak the schema, serialize lazy relations at the worst moment, and make every column rename an API break.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Spring Security is powerful and configures nothing useful by default.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: One model, written down. Mixing method and URL security puts the answer in two places.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A route that appears protected by a URL rule while the method is callable from elsewhere is how internal endpoints leak.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Maven and Gradle both work and a repository should have exactly one.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Whichever wrapper the repository already contains.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Two build definitions drift, and CI ends up building something different from what developers build.

operability.observability: Spring Boot Actuator exposes health and metrics, and Micrometer is the instrumentation seam. A @ControllerAdvice handler is where an unhandled exception becomes a recorded, shaped error instead of a bare 500.
operability.authorization: Spring Security, via method security or URL rules. An endpoint with neither is public, and looks exactly like one that is public on purpose.
done_checks: the application boots with the production profile
clean clone and build from scratch
rules: Every endpoint states its authorization decision, including 'public on purpose'.
Every outbound client has a connect and a read timeout. A RestTemplate with no timeouts waits indefinitely and exhausts the thread pool.
A @ControllerAdvice handler reports unhandled exceptions. Without one they become 500s with no record.
Configuration is validated at startup with @ConfigurationProperties and validation, so a missing value fails the deploy rather than the first request.
Schema changes ship as versioned, reversible migrations. Never rely on ddl-auto in anything past a prototype.

dead_code_risks: Beans instantiated by component scan and never imported by name
Classes referenced only from application.yml or application.properties
JPA entities discovered by package scan
Anything reachable only by reflection, including Jackson serialization targets
Flyway or Liquibase migration files discovered by directory scan
Beans activated by a @Profile or @ConditionalOnProperty that is currently off
